sections.report:
**Section.** The whole piece: applies.

**Findings**
1. **Within one screen or image, does each kind of element look the same everywhere it appears?** No. There are two body paragraphs side by side. The left one (about x 100–600, y 200–365) is set at roughly 22 px with loose leading. The right one (about x 670–1170, y 200–305) is roughly 17 px with tighter leading. They share a font, colour and top edge, so they look like the same kind of element, but one seems to come from a different stylesheet. A viewer reads the right column as a footnote or caption. Its leading also doesn't match the left column's, so the baselines across the gutter never line up and the spread looks unfinished rather than intended. This costs the most because the right column holds the piece's only ask: Thursday evenings, no experience needed, come and help. The styling tells the viewer that the invitation is the least important thing on the page. This breaks the rule that elements of one kind share one style, and a variant appears only where the rules call for it (Gerstner, *Designing Programmes*). Fix: set both paragraphs at one size and leading. If the volunteer paragraph should stand apart, mark it on purpose in a way that lifts it rather than shrinks it, such as a short lead-in heading or a different weight, and keep it at body size. Defect / convention. Weight: major.

**What's working.**
- One serif family carries the headline and both paragraphs, in near-black on white with no ornament. Together they give the plain, quiet, slightly old-fashioned mood that suits a note about varnish, tar and cedar. Keep that restraint when revising.
- The headline "Notes from the boat shed" says exactly what the page holds: informal notes from one specific place. The concrete copy ("clinker dinghies wait on trestles", "a spare apron on the hook by the door") makes the piece clearly someone's own and not a template.

**Couldn't judge from a still.** I can't see how the two columns reflow on a narrow screen. If they stack, the smaller volunteer paragraph would come after the larger one and read as an afterthought even more. Check this on a phone-width viewport.

A note outside the checklist (copy, for the director): the ask names a day but not a time or place. "Thursday evenings" and "the end of the lane" leave a stranger unable to turn up. If recruiting volunteers is part of the job, add a time and a place they can find, such as a street name or a "how to find us" line.

**Checklist.** The whole piece: 8 lines, 7 yes, 1 no (each kind of element looks the same everywhere it appears), 0 unsure

**Section.** What matters first: applies.

**Findings**
1. **"Below the first element, can you tell each level of the text (title, headings, body, captions) from the next at a glance, with no two sizes almost the same?"**: No.
   - **Where:** The two body paragraphs sit side by side, both starting at y ≈ 200. The left one ("The shed sits at the end of the lane…", x 100–600, y 200–365) looks about 22 px. The right one ("Volunteers meet on Thursday evenings…", x 670–1170, y 200–305) looks about 17 px. Both use the same serif, weight and dark grey, and neither has a heading role.
   - **What the viewer experiences:** The difference is big enough to notice but not big enough to explain itself. Nothing else (weight, colour, a label, a rule) says why one paragraph is larger. So the right paragraph doesn't read as a separate level. It reads like a mismatch, or like small print to skip. It also holds the only practical information and the only ask on the page: when to come, that no experience is needed, and the invitation to help. The size step demotes exactly the part a reader would act on, and its baselines don't line up with the left column.
   - **Why:** This matches "Sizes come from a scale" almost exactly: two blocks of ordinary paragraph text in one face and weight, one a little larger, not matching side by side. Bringhurst, *The Elements of Typographic Style*, 3.1.1: "limit yourself… to a modest set of distinct and related intervals." Dair, *Design with Type*, ch. 8: a contrast meant as a difference has to be obvious, or it looks like an accident.
   - **Fix direction:** Decide whether the two paragraphs are the same level. If they are, set both at one body size. If one is meant to stand apart, make the difference unmistakable and give it a reason. The left paragraph could be a clearly larger lede. Or the volunteer paragraph could be marked as its own block, with a short heading, a weight or colour change, or a boxed aside. Either way, it should not lose the weight contest.
   - **Kind:** defect. **Weight:** major, because the size step pushes the volunteer ask to the bottom of the order.

**What's working.**
- **The headline:** It is the single clear starting point. It is bold and about two and a half times the body size, with nothing near it competing, so the eye lands there immediately.
- **Headline against body:** The headline differs from the body in weight as well as size, so the step between them reads as deliberate.

**Checklist.** What matters first: 3 lines, 2 yes, 1 no (text levels distinct, no two sizes almost the same)

I've finished reading the checklist entries and am writing the report now.

**Section.** Arrangement and space: applies. It is a single-screen text page (about 1280×800) with a headline and two text columns. Bash was blocked, so I took no crops and worked from the whole image.

**Findings**
1. **Does the visual weight balance, with no side, crowded or empty, that makes the page look about to tip?** (This also covers the line on deliberate negative space.)
   - **Where:** All the content sits between y ≈ 95 and y ≈ 365. The ~430 px band below it, more than half the frame, is empty from edge to edge. The right column ends even higher, at y ≈ 305, so the lower right is the emptiest part. The left also carries more weight: a wider headline (to x ≈ 730), larger type and five lines against four.
   - **What the viewer sees:** The page looks top-heavy and unfinished, as if something failed to load below the text or the layout was never closed off. The empty area is not shaped and sets nothing off, so it reads as leftover space rather than a place to rest.
   - **Why:** Arnheim, *Art and Visual Perception*, ch. I "Balance": weight comes from size, darkness and position, and a heavy side needs a counterweight. The entry "Negative space is deliberate" (Tschichold; Müller-Brockmann) names "large unexplained empty areas" as a fault.
   - **Fix:** Either give the empty space a job or remove it.
     - If this is the whole piece, shrink the frame to fit the content, or move the text block lower so the white space gathers around it on purpose.
     - If this is a web page, end it with something that anchors the bottom. The volunteer invitation is the obvious candidate, with the meeting time and a way to join.
   - **Marks:** Convention. Major, because the unfinished look is most of what a viewer takes away from the layout.
2. **Do lines of text in neighboring columns sit on the same baselines?**
   - **Where:** Starting at y ≈ 205, the left column's lines are about 34 px apart and the right column's about 28 px. The first baselines already differ by a few pixels (about 225 against 219). By the third line, the right column's text sits level with the gap between two lines on the left (about 267 against 283).
   - **What the viewer sees:** Reading across the 70 px gutter, the rows don't line up. The two columns look like separate pieces placed side by side, and the near-miss at the top line looks like an error rather than a choice.
   - **Why:** Müller-Brockmann, *Grid Systems in Graphic Design*, "Construction of the grid": neighbouring columns share line intervals.
   - **Fix:** Put both columns on one baseline grid. The simplest way is to set both at one size and leading. If the size difference is meant to rank the two texts, at least make the right column's leading a clean fraction of the left's, and align the first baselines.
   - **Marks:** Convention. Minor.

**What's working.**
- **One clean grid across the page.** A 100 px left margin is shared by the headline and the left column, and the two columns are about 500 px wide each with a ~70 px gutter, which splits the measure cleanly into halves. Keep that structure when you fix the vertical problems.
- **Spacing within and between groups.** The ~60 px gap under the headline is clearly bigger than the line spacing inside the paragraphs, and the gutter clearly separates the two columns. So the headline reads as introducing both, and each column reads as its own group.

**Couldn't judge from a still.** Whether this is the whole page or only the first screen of a longer one. If more content follows below y = 800, the empty band in finding 1 may close up in the live page. Check by scrolling in a browser.

**Checklist.** Arrangement and space: 13 lines, 11 yes, 2 no (lines of text in neighbouring columns share baselines; visual weight balances), 0 unsure. Note: the empty bottom band is filed under balance, so the line on gathered and deliberate white space is answered yes.

sections.report:
Walk (working notes). Bash was refused, so I'm working from the whole image. It is about 1280×800, one screen, so crop.mjs would have printed `no crops` anyway.

First read: the eye lands on the bold serif heading "Notes from the boat shed", then drops to the left paragraph, then to the right paragraph, which is noticeably smaller. It reads as a short editorial or community page about a volunteer boat shed. It feels calm and literary. Job (assumed): a short web article or landing note that describes the shed and invites volunteers.

Text:
1. Body text large enough: yes. Left about 22 px, right about 17 px; there is no menu.
2. Captions and labels: yes (none).
3. Plain reading face: yes.
4. One typeface plan: yes, one serif family.
5. Small text weight: yes.
6. Contrast: yes, near-black on white.
7. Text over image: yes (none).
8. 45–75 characters: yes. Left about 45–52, right about 52–56.
9. Leading suits measure: yes, about 1.5 for both.
10. Multi-line heading: yes (one line).
11. Flush left: yes.
12. Justified: yes (none).
13. Rag: yes, gentle.
14. Widows and runts: yes. Last lines are "and cut cedar hangs in the air all year." and "anyone who wants to help."
15. Heading breaks: yes.
16. Paragraph marks: yes.
17. Left edge crisp: yes.
18. Chunking: yes, the text is short.
19. Mixed case: yes.
20. Emphasis: yes (none).
21. Display tighter: yes. The heading looks set at normal tracking, which works at this weight.
22. Kerning: yes. Nothing gaps or collides in the heading.
23. Text tracking: yes.
24. Caps letterspaced: yes (none).
25. Ligatures: yes, the heading has no fi or fl.
26. Real styles: yes. The heading is a true bold.
27. Quotes and dashes: yes (none present).
28. Tabular figures: yes (none).
29. Real type: yes. It looks like live text, but I can't confirm that from a still.
30. Not clipped: yes.

Nothing is `no` or `unsure`, so step 5 has no entries to open.

**Section.** Text: applies.

**Findings**
None.

This section has no line for one thing, which should go to the hierarchy and type-scale critics. The two body columns use two body sizes: about 22 px on the left (x 100–600, y 200–365) and about 17 px on the right (x 670–1145, y 200–305). They sit side by side, start on the same baseline and do the same job, so the step reads as a mismatch rather than a level. Smaller text usually means "less important", but the right column holds the only invitation on the page ("Volunteers meet on Thursday evenings… anyone who wants to help"). The viewer is told to treat the call to action as secondary. The fix is to set both columns at one body size, or to make the volunteer text plainly a separate element (an aside or a call-out) instead of a slightly smaller twin. This is taste and type scale (Bringhurst; Refactoring UI). Weight: likely major for the invitation, but the director should decide.

**What's working.**
- Both paragraphs sit within a comfortable measure (about 45–56 characters) and use roughly 1.5 leading, with a soft rag and no runts, so each column reads easily in one pass.
- The single serif family (heavy bold for the heading, regular for the text) has a clear contrast in weight without adding a second face. The copy is concrete ("three clinker dinghies wait on trestles", "a spare apron on the hook by the door"), so it couldn't sit on anyone else's page.

**Couldn't judge from a still.** Whether the text is live type and how the two columns reflow on a narrow screen. That matters here because stacking them would make the size mismatch more obvious.

**Checklist.** Text: 30 lines, 30 yes, 0 no, 0 unsure

Walk (Color):
- Small palette: yes. It's one near-black, slightly blue-grey ink on white, with no hue at all.
- Saturated colour kept to a small area: yes. There is none.
- Clear range of light and dark: yes. Dark ink on white keeps the structure in greyscale.
- Warm and cool: yes. There's no warm or cool colour.
- Matching colours look the same: yes. The crop at 560–800 × 200–300 shows both columns in the same ink.
- No vibrating edges: yes.
- Status colours: yes. There are none.
- Meaning shown by colour alone: yes. There is none.
- Dark theme: yes. It's a light page, so this line is met.

**Section.** Color: applies, though the piece is monochrome, with one dark neutral ink on a white ground.

**Findings**
None.

**What's working.** The page uses one ink for everything: the headline, both text columns and the white ground. All the structure comes from size and weight, not colour. On a quiet editorial page like this, nothing competes with the words. The ink is a soft blue-black rather than pure #000, so the type looks crisp on white without glaring. Keep that one colour if the page is revised. If an accent is ever added, for example to pick out the Thursday-evening invitation, keep it to one hue in a small area.

**Checklist.** Color: 9 lines, 9 yes, 0 no, 0 unsure

**Section.** Pictures: skipped. The image has no photos, illustrations, icons, logos or marks. It is only a headline and two text columns on white.

**Findings**
None.

**Couldn't judge from a still.** The bottom half of the page, from about y 370 to 800, is empty white. There is no broken-image icon or placeholder box there, so I can't tell if a picture was meant to go there and didn't load, or if the space is intentional. Check the live page to see whether an image should appear below the columns.

**Checklist.** Pictures: skipped
